items.questionAndWhy: Can brief interface cues help people accept AI answers selectively—distinguishing correct information from incorrect information—instead of simply trusting or rejecting the system?
items.whatTheyDid: A randomized online experiment assigned 800 adults to source-transparency and accuracy-warning conditions in a 2-by-2 between-person design. Each person judged 12 correct and 12 incorrect fixed AI-style answers, producing 19,200 trial observations; the study recorded acceptance and verification.
items.whatTheyFound: Acceptance of incorrect answers was 45% without cues, 36% with source information, 28% with a warning, and 21% with both. Verification was highest with both cues (52%). The correct-versus-incorrect acceptance difference also widened. These are immediate low-risk judgments from an online sample, not high-stakes decisions or live chatbot conversations.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX human–AI analyst interfaces, source display and brief warnings are testable safeguards against inappropriate reliance. Their effects on expert analysis, long-term habituation and operational accuracy remain untested; reducing acceptance alone must be distinguished from improving discrimination.
items.streamTitle: Source information and accuracy warnings reduced erroneous reliance on AI answers
items.streamSummary: An experiment with 800 adults found erroneous-answer acceptance fell from 45% without cues to 21% with both source information and warnings; 52% verified in the combined condition. Results concern low-risk, short-term AI-style judgments.
items.attribution: Xing, Zhang, Zhang et al. — Scientific Reports (randomized online experiment; 14 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Does early visual cortex merely encode threatening cues, or participate causally in the consolidation of persistent fear memories after conditioning?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers combined human fear conditioning, high-definition alpha-frequency transcranial alternating current stimulation over early visual cortex, simultaneous EEG–fMRI and neural decoding. Fear-related representations were assessed approximately 15 minutes, 24 hours and seven days after conditioning.
items.whatTheyFound: Early sensory signals and widespread memory traces appeared across retention assessments. Conditioning altered occipital alpha activity; targeted stimulation changed early visual cortical inhibition and disrupted later consolidation and retention while largely sparing initial acquisition. The causal inference is specific to this stimulation protocol and conditioned fear, not complex real-world threat narratives.
items.whatItMeans: The study distinguishes forming an immediate threat association from retaining it. PSYWERX behavioral research could separately measure immediate response and delayed retention to threatening cues, but extrapolating the neural mechanism to political fear, propaganda or operational influence requires direct human-context tests.
items.streamTitle: Brain stimulation dissociated acquiring fear from maintaining it over a week
items.streamSummary: Human fear-conditioning research used EEG–fMRI and visual-cortex stimulation to find later memory retention could be disrupted while initial acquisition remained intact. The result concerns conditioned fear, not demonstrated narrative persuasion.
items.attribution: Brown, Ma, Wang et al. — Nature Communications (human neural stimulation and longitudinal retention; 14 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Do appearance, conversational intelligence and perceived mental human-likeness relate differently to people's sense of interacting with virtual influencers, and how are those responses associated with purchase intentions?
items.whatTheyDid: An online consumer survey measured three perceived dimensions of virtual-influencer anthropomorphism—physical likeness, interactivity intelligence and mental human-likeness—alongside social presence, telepresence, parasocial relationship and intended purchasing. The authors fitted mediated relationships in survey data.
items.whatTheyFound: All three anthropomorphism dimensions were positively associated with presence-related measures; modeled paths linked presence with parasocial relationships and purchase intention. Because measures were concurrent and self-reported, the proposed mediation is associational, and actual purchasing, long-term relationships and causal effects were not demonstrated.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX research into synthetic communicators, human-like appearance and interactive or mental cues should be separated in measurement and randomized interface trials. Results provide candidate constructs for testing rapport, not evidence that anthropomorphic agents reliably persuade political or operational audiences.
items.streamTitle: Virtual-influencer human-likeness related to parasocial attachment and purchase intentions
items.streamSummary: An online consumer survey associated physical, interactive and mental human-likeness of virtual influencers with presence, parasocial relationships and purchase intention. Causal influence and observed purchases were not measured.
items.attribution: Li, Cheng, Han et al. — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (cross-sectional consumer study; 14 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How can allied forces turn lessons from Ukraine's rapidly changing battlefield into changes in doctrine, training and acquisition quickly enough to keep pace with a learning adversary?
items.whatTheyDid: A 13 November CSIS report by a former commander of SAG-U and NSATU draws on more than 30 visits to Ukraine over two years and engagements with military leaders, frontline units and innovators. It organizes examples of operational adaptation and proposes an observation–learning–adaptation–testing cycle.
items.whatTheyFound: The report describes rapid feedback between Ukrainian operators, engineers and industry and argues Western institutional adoption remains episodic. It proposes shared data, reciprocal experimentation, embedded exchanges and scorecards for actual organizational change. These are practitioner observations and recommendations, not a controlled comparison measuring adaptation speed or combat effects.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX operations and wargame assessment, measure not only identification of lessons but time to changed decisions, training, procedures and tested capabilities. The report supplies an operational learning framework, not validated estimates that faster adaptation alone produces particular combat outcomes.
items.streamTitle: CSIS argued that military advantage depends on institutional learning speed
items.streamSummary: CSIS draws on firsthand Ukraine operational experience to argue that allied learning should be measured from observation through tested institutional change. Its proposed scorecards and exchanges are recommendations, not experimentally proven effects.
items.attribution: Curtis Buzzard — Center for Strategic and International Studies (practitioner operational report; 13 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How effectively do major social platforms detect and remove commercially purchased fake engagement, including newer AI-enabled and paid-advertising variants?
items.whatTheyDid: The NATO StratCom Centre of Excellence conducted its sixth annual social-platform manipulation experiment, deliberately creating nonpolitical posts and purchasing inauthentic engagement from commercial providers. The 2025 evaluation expanded to seven platforms and examined sponsored content and AI-generated posts.
items.whatTheyFound: The report documents continued availability of low-cost inauthentic engagement and uneven removals, with some enforcement improvement. Reported experiments involved more than 30,000 inauthentic accounts and more than 100,000 interactions. Purchased interactions and platform response measure system vulnerability, not whether real people were persuaded. Conditions and providers differ from prior cycles.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX information-environment assessment, count purchased activity, persistence, platform enforcement and authentic-user uptake as different outcomes. This older original field experiment is included for its distinct controlled measurement of manipulation infrastructure, not as a new November incident.
items.streamTitle: NATO's purchased-engagement experiment found persistent manipulation opportunities
items.streamSummary: A NATO StratCom field experiment across seven platforms purchased artificial engagement on nonpolitical posts and found persistent cheap manipulation despite some improved removals. Exposure, belief change and persuasion were not established.
items.attribution: Bergmanis-Korāts, Haiduchyk and Smolts — NATO Strategic Communications Centre of Excellence (2025 platform experiment; published 30 January 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can changing an AI model's decision-style persona alter action recommendations while case evidence remains unchanged, and do such shifts generalize across models and case sets?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers crossed three ethical orientations with three cognitive styles to form nine physician-style prompts, plus a no-persona baseline. Twenty open-weight models answered five binary decisions for 2,500 simulated emergency vignettes and 2,500 real discharge-summary texts, with repeated runs totaling five million model decisions.
items.whatTheyFound: With fixed input evidence, affirmative rates ranged from 36.9% to 46.4% across personas, versus 42.8% unconditioned. Effects differed by autonomy and treatment questions; directional agreement across corpora was 85.7%. Model susceptibility varied, and larger size or medical fine-tuning did not consistently protect against shifts. These are model choices, not measured clinical decisions by human physicians.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX research agents and synthetic personas, configuration prompts must be treated as behavioral parameters subject to regression testing, not cosmetic descriptions. The clinical domain is an evaluation setting; applying the exact response shifts to influence or human choice is untested.
items.streamTitle: System personas shifted AI action thresholds under identical evidence
items.streamSummary: Across 20 LLMs and five million fixed-evidence decisions, changing ethical/cognitive persona prompts shifted affirmative-action rates across a 9.5-point range. This demonstrates AI prompt sensitivity, not human decision behavior.
items.attribution: Klang, Gorenshtein, Omar et al. — npj Health Systems (LLM prompt-controlled evaluation; 14 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can autonomous research agents reliably reconstruct scientific workflows, learn reusable procedures and judge claims using original data rather than persuasive written answers?
items.whatTheyDid: NIBench evaluated 19 language models in a common agent framework. It included 56 neuroimaging workflow tasks across seven tool ecosystems, experiments on procedural-skill distillation, and 36 published Alzheimer's research claims requiring raw-data analysis and reproducible supporting evidence.
items.whatTheyFound: Leading agents could execute explicitly supplied procedures nearly perfectly, but performance separated more when guidance was withheld. Distilled skills helped on acquired procedures with inconsistent transfer to unseen tasks. Agents sometimes produced reproducible outputs while arriving at conclusions differing from expert benchmarks; access to data did not always improve judgment. This is a preprint benchmark in neuroimaging, not a universal agent reliability rate.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX research automation, distinguish procedural execution, transfer to unfamiliar tasks and scientific inference as separate evaluated capabilities. Require verified artifacts and independent claim assessment; the transfer of neuroimaging benchmark results to behavioral research remains a hypothesis.
items.streamTitle: Scientific agents executed protocols more reliably than they judged research claims
items.streamSummary: NIBench compared 19 models on 56 scientific workflows and 36 evidence-based research claims; execution of provided protocols was strong, but transfer and scientific judgment were less reliable. The results are benchmark-specific.
items.attribution: Zhong, Xia, Zhang et al. — arXiv NIBench preprint (research-agent benchmarking; 11 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How could an apparently spontaneous action arise in a neural network with no immediate sensory trigger, and how might pre-movement readiness signals emerge before a decision threshold is reached?
items.whatTheyDid: Researchers built a six-area brain-constrained recurrent neural-network model representing learned perception–action circuits. Without external sensory input, internal stochastic activity sometimes triggered circuit ignition. They compared simulated action waiting times and slow pre-movement neural ramping with previously observed human results.
items.whatTheyFound: For selected parameters, the model reproduced human-like waiting-time distributions and readiness-potential-like ramping prior to simulated movement. This is mechanistic modeling, not an experiment demonstrating that noise-driven ignition actually causes human voluntary action or settles deterministic-versus-stochastic theories. Parameter selection and architecture constrain inference.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX causal behavioral modeling, latent fluctuations and decision thresholds can generate variability in action timing even without a new external stimulus. Treat the mechanism as a testable model class, not proof that human deliberation is random or that operational decisions follow this neural architecture.
items.streamTitle: Brain-constrained simulation reproduced voluntary-action waiting times and readiness signals
items.streamSummary: A six-area neural-network simulation reproduced selected voluntary-action waiting-time patterns and readiness-like ramping through spontaneous circuit ignition. It is a modeled account, not direct confirmation of human neural causation.
items.attribution: Griffin, Schurger and Garagnani — Scientific Reports (brain-constrained neural simulation; 14 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: How should a model choose actions when other actors are neither perfectly predictable strategic optimizers nor fully adversarial, and their actual policies may be misspecified?
items.whatTheyDid: A November 12 preprint formulated strategically robust dynamic equilibrium in dynamic games, interpolating between game-theoretic and robust-control assumptions. Authors analyzed open- and closed-loop settings and conducted numerical experiments in vehicle platooning, inventory and network control.
items.whatTheyFound: The formal framework models policy misspecification explicitly and reports resilience and some computational benefits in the tested numerical settings. Certain simulated cases improved performance or social welfare. These are mathematical and engineering simulations; no actual human populations, bargaining behavior or influence responses were tested.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX COA comparison, opponent-policy uncertainty could be represented separately from environmental uncertainty and sensitivity-tested across adversary models. The transfer is specific and plausible but unvalidated: the engineering equilibrium does not establish human strategic decision rules.
items.streamTitle: Strategically robust games modeled uncertainty about other agents' policies
items.streamSummary: A new dynamic-game formulation explicitly hedged against misspecified policies of other agents and improved robustness in selected numerical control simulations. Human strategic and behavioral applicability remains untested.
items.attribution: Velasevic, Lanzetti and Mazumdar — arXiv preprint (formal multi-agent control and numerical experiments; 12 November 2026)

items.questionAndWhy: Can longitudinally organized cross-sectional surveys track family-related outcomes through social unrest, pandemic disruption and later recovery, enabling contextual comparisons instead of single-year snapshots?
items.whatTheyDid: A new Scientific Data descriptor releases harmonized self-report and demographic records from 7,744 Hong Kong respondents collected in 2019–2025 through online or face-to-face methods. Coverage includes social unrest, pandemic and post-pandemic periods, with documented validation and index variables.
items.whatTheyFound: The concrete contribution is a reusable multi-period dataset rather than a new causal estimate of unrest or pandemic effects. Sample composition and collection modes can differ between periods, and the available data do not establish within-person changes, representative national comparisons or intervention effects.
items.whatItMeans: For PSYWERX cross-cultural behavior measurement, the dataset could support exploratory analyses of relationships among family wellbeing, social connection and contextual disruption, with careful adjustment for survey-wave differences. It is enabling data infrastructure, not evidence of a validated influence mechanism.
items.streamTitle: A 2019–2025 Hong Kong family-wellbeing dataset enables comparisons across disruptions
items.streamSummary: A Scientific Data release covers 7,744 Hong Kong respondents across 2019–2025 unrest, pandemic and recovery periods, with harmonized family-wellbeing variables. The data permit contextual comparisons but not automatic causal attribution.
items.attribution: Lam, Odetayo, Chan et al. — Scientific Data (multi-period public dataset descriptor; 14 November 2026)
